alt: Four questions with bars sized by marks: Question 1 (3 marks, AO1) shows knowledge; Question 2 (6) explains one way; Question 3 (9) explains two ways or reasons; Question 4 (12) explains a given factor and at least one other and judges their relative importance. Allow about 50 minutes, about 18 for the 12-mark question.
caption: From knowledge to explanation to judgement as the marks rise.

after: ## Option 1: The origins of the First World War, c1890-1915
alt: A schematic of alliances. Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy form the Triple Alliance of 1882. France and Russia are linked by the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894, Britain and France by the Entente Cordiale of 1904, and Britain and Russia by the Anglo-Russian Agreement of 1907. A note says Britain left Splendid Isolation and Italy did not join its partners in 1914.
caption: Two groupings formed by 1907; Britain ended its isolation as rivalry with Germany grew.

after: ## Option 1: The origins of the First World War, c1890-1915
alt: A sequence: Franz Ferdinand assassinated on 28 June 1914; Austria-Hungary's ultimatum only partly accepted; war on Serbia on 28 July; Russia mobilises; Germany declares war on Russia and France; the Schlieffen Plan sends troops through Belgium; Britain declares war on 4 August as a guarantor of Belgian neutrality; the Ottoman Empire and Italy join later.
caption: Each step drew in another power: alliances and the Schlieffen Plan turned a Balkan war into a world war.

after: ## Option 2: Hitler's foreign policy and the origins of the Second World War, 1933-1941
alt: A timeline of Hitler's foreign policy: leaving the League (1933), the pact with Poland (1934), the Saar and conscription (1935), the Rhineland (March 1936), the Anschluss (March 1938), Munich (September 1938), the occupation of Czechoslovakia (March 1939), the Nazi-Soviet Pact (23 August 1939), the invasion of Poland and declarations of war (September 1939), and the widening of the war in 1941.
caption: Step by step from leaving the League to war, with March 1939 ending appeasement.

after: ## Option 3: The origins and development of the Cold War, 1945-1960
alt: Four action-and-reaction rows: the Truman Doctrine (1947) and the Soviet creation of Cominform; Marshall Aid (1947), rejected by the USSR, which set up Comecon; the new currency in the Western zones (1948) and the Berlin Blockade, answered by the Airlift; and NATO (1949) alongside two German states and the first Soviet atomic test.
caption: Each Western move met a Soviet response, deepening the division of Europe.

after: ## Option 4: Détente and the collapse of communism, c1969-1991
alt: Four phases left to right: détente, with SALT I and the Helsinki Accords; the collapse of détente after the invasion of Afghanistan, with boycotts and SDI; a second détente under Gorbachev, with Reykjavik and START; and the collapse of communism, with the opening of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the end of the USSR in December 1991.
caption: Détente, renewed tension, a second détente, then collapse.

alt: Two panels, one per reason. Reason 1: the division of Germany and the Berlin Blockade, with precise detail (the 1948 currency, the blockade and airlift) and a link (Germany as a test of strength, leading to NATO and two German states). Reason 2: the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Aid, with detail and a link (Europe divided economically as well as politically).
caption: Name each reason, support it with precise detail, then link it to why tension rose.

alt: A plan for a 12-mark answer: the given factor, alliances, drew Russia, Germany and France into the Austro-Serbian war. Four other factors: the Schlieffen Plan, the naval race and imperial rivalry, Balkan nationalism, and leaders' decisions. The judgement weighs them: alliances were the framework, but planning made escalation rapid and Belgium decided Britain's entry.
caption: Explain the given factor and at least one other, then judge which mattered more and why.
